finding.claim: purge() calls checkPerm(u, "admin") but discards its boolean result, so the destructive purgeAll() runs for any user object present in the request context, regardless of permissions.
finding.source: Request reaching the purge route with a user object in its context (userFrom, handlers.go:40). No admin permission is required. Whether unauthenticated callers can reach it depends on routing/auth middleware, which is not in this directory.
finding.sink: purgeAll() at handlers.go:27 (destructive bulk operation; body is an empty stub in this file, so real impact depends on its implementation elsewhere).

trace.note: purge(w, r) is the HTTP handler.
u := userFrom(r) reads the user from request context.
userFrom does an unchecked type assertion; panics if no user is present (not a bypass; net/http recovers per request).
checkPerm(u, "admin") result is discarded. This is the defect.
checkPerm returns u.Perms[perm] correctly; it is unused, not broken.

finding.guards_checked: checkPerm return value (not enforced, the defect). mustPerm (not called in purge; correctly used in rotateKeys at handlers.go:33). userFrom panic on missing context (not an authz bypass). Route-level auth middleware (not present in this file; unverified). Fix: replace line 26 with `if !mustPerm(w, u, "admin") { return }`.

verdict.guard_found: none. checkPerm (handlers.go:12-14) returns a bool, but the call at handlers.go:26 is a bare statement and the result is discarded. mustPerm (handlers.go:16-22) is not called in purge(); it is used correctly only in rotateKeys (handlers.go:33). userFrom (handlers.go:40) panics on a missing user, which is a crash rather than an authorization check. Route-level middleware is not in this directory, so it is unverified, but nothing visible in this file blocks the call.
verdict.reason: The admin check at handlers.go:26 is a bare checkPerm(u, "admin") call whose bool is discarded, so purgeAll() at handlers.go:27 runs for any user present in the request context, while rotateKeys at handlers.go:33 shows the intended mustPerm pattern. The attacker only needs to be a logged-in low-privilege user, and the only unverified piece is whether route middleware blocks such users, which is not an authorization check in this code.
